theme: Agents that pay, metrics that mislead

questions.concept: Capturing a hidden trip requirement at booking (luggage-fit vehicles)
questions.question: A ride-hailing app sees a high rate of cancelled airport pickups. Interviews show that families with several suitcases often get a small hatchback, the bags don't fit, and the driver or rider cancels at the kerb. What is the best first product change?
options: Ask riders on airport trips how many large bags they have and match only vehicles with enough boot space, pricing that option where needed
Show the vehicle model on the booking screen so riders can judge for themselves whether their bags will fit before the car arrives
Add a cancellation fee for riders who cancel at the kerb so drivers are compensated for the wasted trip to the terminal
Push all airport riders to the SUV category by default, because a bigger car removes the luggage problem for everyone
questions.explanation: The root cause is a requirement (luggage volume) the system never captures, so matching is blind to it. Asking for it only on airport trips, where it matters, keeps friction low for everyone else and lets dispatch match supply that can actually do the job. Pricing a larger vehicle where needed keeps the marketplace balanced.
rationales: Correct: it captures the missing constraint at the moment of intent and uses it in matching, fixing the cause rather than the symptom.
Showing the model pushes the judgement onto riders who rarely know boot sizes, and the mismatch is still discovered too late to rebook easily.
A fee punishes riders for a failure the system created and does nothing to get the family a car their bags fit in.
Defaulting everyone to SUVs overcharges solo travellers and strains a scarcer supply pool, solving one segment's problem at everyone's expense.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers reward candidates who trace a metric problem (cancellations) to a missing piece of information in the flow. Asking for it narrowly, only where it matters, shows you weigh friction against fit.

questions.concept: Early pincode serviceability check to avoid late-funnel disappointment
questions.question: An Indian D2C furniture brand ships to only about 60% of pincodes. Many users add items to the cart and only learn at the address step that delivery isn't available. What is the best fix?
options: Let users enter or auto-detect their pincode on the product page and show delivery availability and date before they add to cart
Keep the address step as it is but add a friendly apology message and a link to browse other products
Hide the product catalogue entirely until users create an account and enter a full delivery address
Show a banner on the home page listing the states the brand delivers to, so users can check before browsing
questions.explanation: Users invest effort browsing and building a cart, so learning about a blocker at the last step is the most frustrating moment possible. Moving the serviceability check to the product page, with a pincode lookup, tells users early and lets the brand show delivery dates that help conversion for serviceable users.
rationales: Correct: it surfaces the constraint at the decision point, before effort is wasted, and doubles as a delivery-date promise for serviceable users.
An apology at the end does not change the wasted effort; the disappointment still lands at the worst point.
Forcing an account and address before browsing adds heavy friction for the majority who can be served.
State-level lists are too coarse when coverage varies by pincode, so users would still be surprised at checkout.
questions.interview_tip: A common product-sense move is 'shift the bad news earlier'. Naming where in the journey the user is most invested, and moving the check before it, is a crisp signal of user empathy.

questions.concept: Exchange-first returns flow to meet the need while keeping the sale
questions.question: A fashion marketplace's return rate is high, and most returns are for the wrong size. The current flow only offers a refund. Which change best serves customers and the business?
options: When the reason is size, offer an instant exchange for the right size first, shipped before the original is collected, with refund still one tap away
Remove the size-related reason from the return form so customers pick a reason that the marketplace can contest
Make refunds take longer than exchanges so that customers are nudged toward choosing an exchange instead
Charge a small return fee on all size-related returns to discourage customers from ordering items casually
questions.explanation: The customer's real need is usually the right item, not their money back. Offering a fast exchange first, with refund still easy, solves that need and keeps the sale. Shipping the replacement before pickup removes the wait that makes people prefer a refund.
rationales: Correct: it matches the dominant reason with the solution that meets the need, keeps the sale, and preserves choice.
Hiding the true reason corrupts the data the team needs and frustrates customers with an obvious dark pattern.
Slowing refunds on purpose is a coercive pattern that erodes trust and invites complaints.
A blanket fee reduces returns by punishing customers for a size problem the marketplace can help solve, and hurts conversion.
questions.interview_tip: Strong product-sense answers separate the request (a refund) from the need (a garment that fits). Showing you can serve the need while protecting revenue, without dark patterns, signals mature judgement.

questions.concept: Guaranteeing early feedback to retain new creators
questions.question: On a short-video app, new creators whose first three posts get almost no views rarely post again. Leadership wants to improve new-creator retention. Which approach best targets the cause?
options: Guarantee each new creator's first few posts a small, relevant test audience so they receive real views and feedback, then let normal ranking take over
Send new creators a weekly email with tips on lighting, hooks and hashtags so they can make posts that rank better
Add a creator badge after the first post to reward people for publishing, regardless of how the post performs
Rank all new creators' posts at the top of the feed for their first month so every post gets high reach
questions.explanation: The drop-off comes from a missing early reward: posting into silence. A small, relevant test audience guarantees real signal and some feedback for every new creator, without breaking feed quality, and it also gives the ranker data to judge the content. Then normal ranking decides reach.
rationales: Correct: it fixes the missing feedback loop at low cost to viewers and gives the ranker the data it needs.
Tips help some creators, but they don't change the experience of posting to zero views, which is what drives the drop-off.
A badge is a hollow reward; creators want an audience, not a symbol, so retention barely moves.
Forcing all new posts to the top hurts viewers with unvetted content and is not sustainable at scale.
questions.interview_tip: Two-sided products come up often at Meta and Google. Name the side you're serving, protect the other side's experience, and show you understand the creator's motivation loop.

questions.concept: Adoption rate inflated by making a feature default-on
questions.question: A notes app turns its new auto-backup feature on by default. 'Feature adoption' jumps from 12% to 85% overnight. What is the most accurate reading?
options: The jump mostly reflects the default change; value should be judged by outcomes such as restores used and opt-out rate
Users clearly love auto-backup, since 85% of them now use it, so the team should promote it more widely
The metric is broken and should be deleted, because default-on features can never be measured meaningfully
The jump proves the earlier onboarding was poor, since most users wanted backup but couldn't find it
questions.explanation: When a feature becomes default-on, 'adoption' measures the default, not user choice. Better signals are whether users keep it on (opt-out rate) and whether it delivers value (restores performed, data-loss tickets falling).
rationales: Correct: it separates the mechanical effect of the default from the evidence of value.
Usage that requires no action isn't evidence of preference; most users never touch defaults.
Default-on features can be measured well; you just need outcome and opt-out metrics instead of adoption.
The data doesn't show users wanted it before; a default jump says nothing about earlier discoverability.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who ask 'what does this metric measure after the change?' Calling out that defaults change the meaning of adoption shows metric literacy.

questions.concept: Auto-replay loops inflating short-video watch time
questions.question: A short-video app makes videos loop automatically. Average watch time per video rises 30%, but likes, shares and follows per view are flat. What is the best interpretation?
options: Much of the gain is likely passive replays while the screen is unattended, so watch time is now a weaker signal of interest
Users are enjoying videos 30% more, so the ranker should weight watch time even more heavily from now on
Likes and shares lag watch time by several weeks, so the team should wait for them to catch up
Watch time and engagement measure the same thing, so the flat engagement must come from a logging bug
questions.explanation: Looping adds time without any user decision, so watch time rises even if nobody is paying more attention. Flat active signals (likes, shares, follows) suggest the extra time is passive. The team should count distinct completions or active rewatches and lean on active signals in ranking.
rationales: Correct: the mechanism adds time without intent, and the flat active signals support that.
Feeding inflated watch time into ranking would reward videos that are left playing, not videos people like.
There is no reason active engagement would lag by weeks; these actions happen during the view.
Watch time and engagement are different signals; diverging is expected when only one is mechanically boosted.
questions.interview_tip: When a UI change mechanically inflates a metric, interviewers want you to say so and propose a cleaner version. Pairing a passive metric with active signals is a strong habit.

questions.concept: Moving friction later shifts drop-off rather than removing it
questions.question: A lending app moves its document upload step from screen 2 to screen 6. Conversion from screen 2 to 3 jumps from 55% to 90% and the team celebrates. What should you check first?
options: End-to-end conversion from start to approved loan, since the same drop-off may simply have moved to the new upload step
Whether screen 3's conversion improved too, since the success of screen 2 should carry through to every later step
How long users now spend on screen 2, since less time on that step proves the flow got easier overall
Whether the jump holds for a week, since step-level gains are reliable once they survive novelty effects
questions.explanation: Moving a hard step later improves the step it left, but users may still abandon when they reach it. Only end-to-end conversion shows whether friction was removed or just moved. Sometimes moving it later helps because users are more invested, but you have to measure the whole funnel to know.
rationales: Correct: the step metric is guaranteed to look better; the full-funnel number is the real test.
Screen 3 isn't where the upload moved, so it can improve while the new upload step loses everyone.
Less time on screen 2 is expected when you remove work from it; it says nothing about overall completion.
A step-level gain can last forever and still be meaningless if the loss reappears later in the funnel.
questions.interview_tip: In metrics rounds, step-level wins are a classic trap. Always zoom out to the end-to-end outcome; it shows you think in systems, not screens.

questions.concept: North Star for a podcast app
questions.question: Which is the best North Star metric for a podcast listening app?
options: Weekly listeners who play most of at least one episode
Total number of podcast shows in the catalogue
Number of app downloads from the app store each month
Total follows of shows across all registered users
questions.explanation: A good North Star captures users getting the core value. For a podcast app that's listening to episodes, measured weekly to match the release cadence. Requiring most of an episode filters out accidental plays.
rationales: Correct: it measures real listening, matches the natural weekly frequency, and filters accidental plays.
Catalogue size is an input on the supply side; users can ignore most of it.
Downloads measure acquisition, not whether people get value and keep coming back.
Follows are cheap to give and often unused; many followed shows are never played.
questions.interview_tip: For North Star questions, say what the core value is, then pick a frequency that matches natural use. Explaining why you filter out low-quality actions earns extra credit.

questions.concept: Pre-set harm stopping boundary for early termination
questions.question: You're launching a test of a new checkout flow that could break payments. You plan to run it for two weeks. How should you handle the risk of serious harm during the test?
options: Agree before launch on a guardrail threshold (for example, payment failures above a set level) that stops the test early, while the ship decision waits for the full run
Check the primary metric daily and stop the test as soon as it shows a significant win, so users get the better flow sooner
Avoid looking at any data until the two weeks are over, so the result is not biased by peeking
Stop the test whenever the treatment looks worse on any metric on any day, to be as safe as possible
questions.explanation: Stopping early for harm and stopping early for success are different. A pre-agreed harm threshold on a guardrail protects users without biasing the ship decision. The ship decision still waits for the planned sample unless you use a proper sequential method.
rationales: Correct: it protects users with a pre-set rule and keeps the main read valid.
Stopping on the first significant win is the peeking problem and inflates false positives.
Never looking risks leaving a broken payments flow live for two weeks.
With many metrics and daily checks, some will look worse by chance, so this rule would stop almost every test.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like hearing that you separate safety monitoring from the decision readout. Naming the guardrail and threshold upfront shows experiment rigour.

questions.concept: Small treatment share understates network-dependent features
questions.question: You test a 'see which friends are going' feature for events with 5% of users in treatment. Lift in RSVPs is tiny and not significant. Why might this understate the feature's real impact?
options: Most treated users' friends are in control and don't show up, so the feature rarely has enough friend data to work
The 5% share makes the test too short, since smaller arms always need more calendar time to reach a stable estimate
Users in control can see the feature through screenshots, which pushes their behaviour toward treatment
Small treatment arms are more affected by novelty effects, which hide the real long-run impact of features
questions.explanation: The feature's value depends on how many of a user's friends also have it and act on it. At 5%, few friends are treated, so the feature is thin. Cluster randomization by friend groups or a geo test gives a more realistic read.
rationales: Correct: the treatment's strength depends on the treatment share, so a small arm understates it.
Arm size affects power, but the real problem is that the feature itself works poorly when few friends have it.
Screenshot leakage is unlikely to be big and would not explain why treated users see so little value.
Novelty effects don't depend on arm size, and novelty usually inflates rather than hides early lift.
questions.interview_tip: Social features break the usual A/B assumptions. Explaining how density changes the treatment and proposing cluster or geo randomization is a strong signal at Meta.

questions.concept: Annual household cooking-oil consumption in Delhi
questions.question: Roughly how many litres of cooking oil do households in Delhi use in a year?
options: About 3 crore litres
About 30 crore litres
About 300 crore litres
About 3,000 crore litres
questions.explanation: Delhi has about 2 crore people, or roughly 50 lakh households of four. A household of four uses around 4–5 litres of oil a month, about 55 litres a year. 50 lakh × 55 L is about 27.5 crore litres, so about 30 crore. A cross-check per person: around 14 litres a year at home × 2 crore people gives about 28 crore.
rationales: This implies about 1.5 litres per person per year, far below what Indian home cooking uses.
Correct: households × monthly use × 12, cross-checked per person, lands near 30 crore litres.
This implies about 150 litres per person a year, roughly 400 ml a day, which is far too much.
This is roughly 100 times too high and would exceed a large share of India's total edible oil use.
questions.interview_tip: In estimation, interviewers watch the structure and a sanity check. Doing both a household and a per-person path, and showing they agree, is what strong candidates do.

questions.concept: LLM cost to generate descriptions for a product catalogue
questions.question: You want an LLM to rewrite descriptions for 2 lakh products. Each call uses about 400 input tokens and 250 output tokens. The model costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Roughly what will one pass cost?
options: About $70
About $700
About $7,000
About $70,000
questions.explanation: Input: 2,00,000 × 400 = 8 crore tokens = 80M tokens × $2/M = $160. Output: 2,00,000 × 250 = 50M tokens × $10/M = $500. Total about $660, or roughly $700. Output tokens drive most of the cost even though there are fewer of them.
rationales: This is about ten times too low; it would drop either the token count or the per-million prices.
Correct: $160 for input plus $500 for output is about $660.
This is about ten times too high, which usually comes from treating 2 lakh as 2 million.
This would need roughly a hundred times more tokens or much higher prices.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM loops often include quick cost math. Writing out tokens × price for input and output separately, and noticing which one dominates, shows you can reason about unit economics.

questions.concept: Charging the merchant side in agentic checkout
questions.question: You run an AI shopping assistant that can complete purchases for users. You need to choose who pays for the checkout service. Which approach usually makes most sense early on?
options: Keep it free for users and charge merchants a fee on completed sales, since merchants get incremental orders and users are the side you must attract
Charge users a monthly fee for checkout, since they get the convenience and merchants will refuse any new fees
Charge both sides the same fee from day one so the business is profitable immediately and neither side feels favoured
Charge merchants a large fixed listing fee upfront, whether or not they get sales, to fund growth quickly
questions.explanation: In two-sided markets you usually subsidise the side that is harder to attract and more price sensitive, and charge the side that gets measurable value. Merchants already pay for sales through ads and payment fees, so a fee on completed orders matches their existing economics and only charges when value is delivered.
rationales: Correct: it subsidises the hard-to-win side and charges a performance-based fee to the side with clear incremental value.
Charging users adds friction where adoption is the main risk, and merchants routinely pay for sales today.
Charging both early slows the network from forming; profitability today matters less than building both sides.
Fixed fees with no sales are a hard sell to merchants who aren't yet sure the channel works.
questions.interview_tip: In strategy rounds, say which side is harder to attract and which captures measurable value. Then match the pricing to that, preferably tied to outcomes.

questions.concept: Judging whether a market tends to winner-take-all
questions.question: Your CEO argues the company must 'win the whole market' in a new B2B category before competitors do. Which signal most suggests the market will NOT be winner-take-all?
options: Customers easily use several vendors at once and switching between them costs little
The leading vendor has a much larger sales team than any of its competitors
The category is growing fast and new competitors are getting venture funding
Most customers say the product is important to them in surveys
questions.explanation: Winner-take-all markets usually have strong network effects, high switching costs, and little multi-homing. If customers easily use several vendors and switching is cheap, the leader can't lock in the market, and several players can thrive. Then focusing on a profitable niche can beat a costly race for share.
rationales: Correct: easy multi-homing and low switching costs prevent one vendor from capturing the whole market.
A larger sales team is a resource advantage but doesn't change the market structure.
Fast growth and funding show attractiveness, not whether the market will consolidate.
Importance to customers says nothing about whether they'll concentrate on a single vendor.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers test whether you can question a 'must win everything' premise. Naming the structural factors (network effects, switching costs, multi-homing) is a strong answer.

questions.concept: Losing default status via a choice-screen mandate
questions.question: A regulator will require phones to show users a choice screen for their default AI assistant, ending your assistant's pre-installed default status. What is the strongest strategic response?
options: Invest in being the best choice at the moment of selection and in deep features users miss once gone, so you win the screen and keep users after
Lobby to delay the rule and keep relying on the default, since default placement has always been the main driver of usage
Pay phone makers more for prominent placement on the choice screen, since the ranking order will decide most choices
Cut investment in the assistant, because once the default is gone the market will fragment and no assistant can win
questions.explanation: Choice screens move the battle from distribution to preference. The response that lasts is to be clearly better at the moment of choice, with a clear pitch, and to build value that keeps users after they pick. Delaying or buying placement may work briefly, but regulators usually design choice screens to limit paid ordering.
rationales: Correct: it competes on the new basis (user preference) and builds retention, which lasts regardless of rules.
Delay doesn't change the long-run shift, and it doesn't fix weak preference if users had only used the product by default.
Choice screens are often randomised or rule-bound, so buying order is usually limited or not allowed.
Losing a default doesn't mean nobody can win; many users still choose a clear favourite.
questions.interview_tip: Regulatory shifts show up in strategy rounds. Strong candidates reframe what the new competition is about and invest there, instead of fighting the rule.

questions.concept: Bias in public feature-voting boards
questions.question: Your B2B SaaS product has a public feature-voting board. The top-voted request has 900 votes. Why should you be careful about simply building it next?
options: Votes overrepresent vocal, free or small users and say little about revenue, severity or strategic fit, so weigh them with other evidence
Votes on public boards are usually fake, so the team should ignore the board and rely only on internal opinions
The top request has already been seen by competitors, so building it gives no advantage and wastes effort
Voting boards always lag behind current needs by a year, so the top items no longer reflect what users want
questions.explanation: Voting boards capture people who visit and vote, which skews toward engaged, vocal users and often free plans. They don't show how severe the problem is, how much revenue is involved, or whether it fits strategy. Treat votes as one input next to interviews, usage data and account value.
rationales: Correct: it names the sampling bias and what votes leave out, and keeps the board as one input.
Votes aren't usually fake; the issue is who votes, not whether votes are real.
Competitor visibility doesn't make solving a real customer problem worthless.
Boards can be current; the issue is representativeness, not a fixed lag.
questions.interview_tip: Prioritisation questions often test whether you can spot biased inputs. Saying who is missing from the data, and what you'd add, shows judgement.

questions.concept: Geofencing a launch around a late regulatory blocker
questions.question: Two weeks before a global launch, legal says one feature may breach a new rule in one EU country, pending review. Marketing is booked worldwide. What is the best plan?
options: Launch everywhere else on schedule with the feature turned off in that country, and switch it on there if legal clears it
Delay the whole global launch until legal finishes reviewing, so every market gets the same experience on the same day
Launch everywhere including that country and fix the issue later if the regulator raises a complaint
Remove the feature from the product in every market so there is no legal risk anywhere
questions.explanation: The risk is limited to one country, so the response should be limited too. Geofencing the feature there keeps the launch on track for everyone else and keeps the option to enable it later. This needs feature flags by region, which is why launch plans should include them.
rationales: Correct: it contains the risk to the affected market and keeps everyone else on schedule.
Delaying everyone over one country's review wastes marketing spend and value elsewhere.
Knowingly launching a possible breach puts the company at legal and reputational risk.
Removing it everywhere gives up value in markets that have no problem.
questions.interview_tip: Execution questions often test whether you can contain risk. Saying 'scope the response to the scope of the problem' is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Measuring a platform migration by consumer teams migrated
questions.question: You lead a project to move internal teams from an old logging system to a new platform. Which success metric best shows the project is working?
options: Share of services sending logs only to the new platform, with the old system's traffic falling to zero
Number of features shipped on the new platform compared with the old system
Number of internal documents and tutorials written about the new platform
Number of engineers who attended the new platform's launch training session
questions.explanation: The goal of a migration is to move users off the old system so it can be turned off. Measuring the share of services fully migrated, and traffic on the old system, tracks that goal directly. Features, docs and training are inputs.
rationales: Correct: it measures the actual outcome, full migration, and points at shutting the old system down.
Features shipped is output, not proof that anyone moved.
Docs help adoption but don't show that teams migrated.
Training attendance is an early input; people can attend and never migrate.
questions.interview_tip: Platform PM questions test whether you measure outcomes for internal customers. Mentioning when you can turn off the old system shows you think about the full cost.

questions.concept: Flagging a peer's launch risk on your own system the day before launch
questions.question: The evening before a peer PM's big launch, you notice their feature will call your team's API at a rate that will likely overload it during peak traffic. They didn't consult your team. What should you do?
options: Contact the peer that night with the data, propose options such as rate limits or a staged ramp, and agree a plan together, escalating only if needed
Say nothing, since they didn't consult you, and let the launch show them they should have involved your team
Quietly add strict rate limits to your API that night so their calls are throttled without bothering them
Email both your managers that night asking them to cancel the launch because of the risk to your system
questions.explanation: Ownership means acting on a risk you can see, even if it's not your launch. Going to the peer directly, with data and ready options, gives them the best chance to launch safely. Escalate only if you can't agree and the risk is serious. Holding back or acting unilaterally both damage the shared outcome and trust.
rationales: Correct: it acts quickly, gives the peer data and options, and keeps escalation as a backup.
Letting a preventable outage happen to teach a lesson hurts customers and the company.
Silent throttling could break their launch in confusing ways and damages trust.
Going to managers first, before talking to the peer, escalates too early and frames it as a blame issue.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon-style questions on Ownership look for action on problems outside your remit. Strong answers talk to the person first, bring options, and protect the customer.

questions.concept: Prioritising requests from your former team after moving roles
questions.question: You recently moved to a platform PM role. Your old team keeps messaging you directly for favours and expects you to put their requests first. Other teams have more urgent needs. What's the best approach?
options: Explain warmly that you now prioritise all teams the same way, route their requests through the standard intake, and help them make a strong case
Keep putting their requests first, since you know their needs best and the relationship is valuable
Stop answering their messages so they learn to use the new process without you
Ask your manager to tell your old team to stop contacting you directly
questions.explanation: Fairness across your customers matters in a platform role. Being direct and kind with your old team, and showing them how to make a strong case through the standard process, keeps the relationship and your credibility with other teams. Favouritism or going silent both cause harm.
rationales: Correct: it's fair to all teams, keeps the relationship, and actually helps your old team succeed through the process.
Favouring your old team undermines trust with other teams and misallocates platform capacity.
Going silent damages a relationship that's still useful and seems unprofessional.
Having your manager handle it avoids a conversation you can have yourself and seems cold.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers look for candidates who handle relationships directly and fairly. Saying how you'd keep the relationship while holding the line shows maturity.

questions.concept: Proposing a shared goal to unblock a misaligned dependency
questions.question: Your launch needs work from a partner team, but it isn't in their goals and they keep deprioritising it. What is the most effective step?
options: Show how the work helps their goals, and if it doesn't, propose with both leads a shared goal or explicit trade-off so the priority is set openly
Keep asking every week until they eventually agree to do the work to stop the reminders
Have your engineers do the work in the partner team's codebase without asking them first
Tell your leadership that the partner team is blocking your launch and let them sort it out
questions.explanation: Teams follow their goals. First check whether the work helps something they care about. If not, the real issue is a priority gap that leaders should resolve, so propose a shared goal or a clear trade-off. This turns a favour into a visible decision.
rationales: Correct: it fixes the incentive gap and gets an open decision rather than relying on pressure.
Repeated asking wears down the relationship and doesn't change their priorities.
Working in their codebase without permission creates ownership and quality problems.
Escalating with blame damages trust and skips trying to align incentives first.
questions.interview_tip: Influence without authority is common in PM loops. Strong answers start with the other team's goals and use escalation as a joint step.

questions.concept: Measuring argument-level accuracy in agent tool calls
questions.question: Your agent books meetings using a calendar tool. Evals show it picks the right tool 98% of the time, but users still complain about wrong bookings. What should you measure next?
options: Whether the arguments passed to the tool, such as date, time zone and attendees, are correct
How fast the agent picks the tool, since slow selection probably leads to booking mistakes
How often the agent uses the tool compared with simply answering in text
How many different tools the agent can choose from in each conversation
questions.explanation: Picking the right tool is only half of a tool call. If arguments such as dates, time zones or attendees are wrong, the booking fails even with the correct tool. Field-level argument accuracy is the metric that matches the user complaint.
rationales: Correct: argument errors explain wrong bookings even when tool choice is right.
Speed doesn't explain wrong bookings; a fast call can still have the wrong date.
Tool use rate doesn't say whether the bookings it makes are right.
The number of tools may affect selection, but selection is already 98% accurate.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews often test whether you break agent quality into steps. Separating tool selection from argument accuracy shows careful eval design.

questions.concept: Cumulative context cost growth in long agent loops
questions.question: An agent that makes 40 tool calls per task costs far more than the team estimated from the cost of one call. Each step re-sends the whole conversation so far. What explains the gap, and what's the best fix?
options: Each step re-reads all earlier steps, so input tokens grow with every call; use prompt caching and summarise or trim old tool output
The model gets more expensive per token as the task continues, so the team should switch to a model with flat pricing
Tool calls are billed separately from tokens, so the fix is to group several tool calls into one bigger call
The agent is using more output tokens per step over time, so the fix is a lower maximum output length
questions.explanation: If each step sends the full history, step n pays for all n−1 earlier steps, so total input grows roughly with the square of the number of steps. Caching the unchanging prefix and trimming or summarising old tool output cut this. Fewer steps also help.
rationales: Correct: it explains the growing input per step and gives the standard fixes.
Per-token prices don't rise during a task; the number of tokens per call does.
The gap comes from tokens re-sent, not a separate fee for tool calls.
Output length per step usually stays similar; the growing input is the real driver.
questions.interview_tip: Cost questions are common in AI PM loops. Explaining why agent cost grows faster than linearly, and naming caching and trimming, shows real experience.

questions.concept: Limits of back-translation for evaluating machine translation
questions.question: To check an AI's English-to-Hindi translations, a team translates the Hindi back to English and compares it with the original. Scores look great. What's the main weakness of this method?
options: A model can produce stiff or wrong Hindi that still translates back cleanly, so native speaker review of the Hindi is still needed
Back-translation always gives low scores, so great scores show the method was set up wrong
It only works for languages that use the Latin alphabet, so it cannot be used for Hindi
It measures speed rather than quality, so it says nothing about how good the translation is
questions.explanation: Back-translation checks whether meaning survives a round trip, not whether the target text reads naturally to a native speaker. Literal or awkward Hindi, or wrong formality, can translate back well. Native speaker review or reference-based scoring on the Hindi is needed.
rationales: Correct: round-trip checks miss fluency and tone in the target language.
Back-translation can score high; high scores don't prove a broken setup.
Script doesn't stop the method; it works across scripts.
It does measure something about meaning, not speed; the issue is what it misses.
questions.interview_tip: Multilingual AI questions test whether you know what an eval actually measures. Naming the gap and proposing native review is a strong answer.

questions.concept: Proactive AI suggestions and interruption cost
questions.question: Your email client's AI now pops up suggestions while users type. Acceptance is 20%, but users also report feeling distracted, and typing speed drops. What's the best next step?
options: Show suggestions only when confidence is high or the user pauses, and measure net time saved, not only acceptance
Show suggestions more often, since more suggestions will lead to more accepted ones
Remove the suggestions, because any distraction means the feature is a failure
Keep the feature as is, since 20% acceptance is a healthy benchmark for AI suggestions
questions.explanation: Proactive AI has a cost each time it interrupts, even when the suggestion is ignored. Showing suggestions only at good moments and when confidence is high cuts that cost. Net time saved captures both benefit and interruption.
rationales: Correct: it reduces interruptions and measures the true net benefit.
More suggestions would increase distraction and may lower net value.
The feature has value for 20% of suggestions; tuning it is better than removing it.
Acceptance alone ignores the cost to users who are distracted.
questions.interview_tip: Strong AI PM answers think about the cost of AI acting proactively. Proposing a net metric that includes interruptions shows good judgement.

questions.concept: Tracking per-item regressions on a model upgrade, not just net win rate
questions.question: A new model wins on 70% of your eval items against the old model and loses on 30%. The team wants to ship. What should you check before deciding?
options: What the 30% losses are, especially whether they cluster in important tasks or segments that the new model now gets wrong
Whether the new model is newer, since newer models are better on average
Whether the win rate is above 50%, since that's enough to prove the new model is better
Whether the new model uses a larger context window than the old one
questions.explanation: Overall win rate can hide serious regressions. If losses cluster in key tasks, users who rely on them get worse results. Reviewing losses by task and segment, and adding them to regression evals, prevents shipping a model that breaks important use cases.
rationales: Correct: it checks where the regressions are and whether they matter.
Being newer doesn't guarantee better results on your product's tasks.
A win rate above 50% doesn't rule out harmful regressions on key tasks.
Context window is a spec, not evidence of better results on your evals.
questions.interview_tip: AI interviews reward candidates who look beyond aggregate metrics. Saying 'I'd examine the losses' shows care for users who might be hurt.

questions.concept: Backpressure when consumers fall behind producers
questions.question: A system puts orders into a queue faster than workers can process them. The queue keeps growing. What is backpressure?
options: A way for the slow consumer to signal producers to slow down or reject work, so the system doesn't get overwhelmed
A technique that compresses messages so more of them fit into the queue at once
A backup that copies the queue to a second region in case the first one fails
A method for retrying failed messages with increasing wait times between attempts
questions.explanation: Backpressure lets a slow part of the system push back on the fast part, by slowing producers, rejecting new work, or shedding load. Without it, queues grow until memory runs out or latency becomes huge.
rationales: Correct: it describes signalling upstream to control the flow.
Compression saves space but doesn't fix a consumer that's too slow.
Copying to another region is about disaster recovery, not flow control.
This describes exponential backoff for retries, not backpressure.
questions.interview_tip: Technical PM questions check whether you know common system ideas. Explaining backpressure in plain words and linking it to user impact is enough.

questions.concept: Clock skew makes cross-server timestamps unreliable for ordering
questions.question: A chat app orders messages by the timestamp each server records. Users sometimes see replies appear before the message they reply to. What's the most likely cause?
options: Server clocks differ slightly, so timestamps from different servers don't reliably show which message came first
The database is storing timestamps in local time instead of UTC, so all messages are shifted
The app has too many users, so the database sorts messages randomly when it is busy
The CDN is caching messages, so newer ones show up before older ones
questions.explanation: Clocks on different servers are never perfectly in sync. If two messages are written by different servers a few milliseconds apart, their timestamps can be out of order. Systems use sequence numbers per conversation or logical clocks to order messages reliably.
rationales: Correct: clock differences between servers can flip the order of close messages.
A UTC mix-up would shift all messages consistently, not swap close ones.
Databases don't sort randomly under load; sorting is deterministic.
CDNs usually cache static content, not real-time chat messages.
questions.interview_tip: This shows up in technical rounds as 'why are things out of order?' Knowing about clock skew and sequence numbers shows good technical judgement.

questions.concept: Referral rewards paid on invites that would have happened anyway
questions.question: A fintech app launches a referral bonus. Referred signups double, but total signups rise only 10%. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Many people who would have joined through word of mouth now come through referral links, so the bonus pays for signups it didn't create
The referral program is working perfectly, since doubling referred signups proves that the program drives growth
Referred users are lower quality, so they'll churn faster and the program should be stopped immediately
The bonus is too small, since a bigger bonus would double total signups as well
questions.explanation: Referral programs often capture existing word of mouth. If total signups grow much less than referred signups, many 'referred' users would have joined anyway. Measuring incremental signups, for example with a holdout, shows true value.
rationales: Correct: it explains the gap between referred and total signups.
Referred signups can rise without adding real growth.
Nothing here says referred users churn faster.
A bigger bonus might just pay more for the same signups.
questions.interview_tip: Growth questions often test incrementality. Saying 'compare total, not just attributed' shows you can see through vanity numbers.

questions.concept: ChatGPT Wallet per-transaction approval for agent purchases (Nov 2026)
questions.question: In November 2026, OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet was reported to let its dots agent make purchases for US ChatGPT Pro subscribers, with card details hidden from the agent and merchant. For now, every transaction needs the user's individual approval, with spending-limit permissions planned later. What's the best product reason to start this way?
options: Agent purchase mistakes are costly and trust is new, so approving each one keeps users safe while the team learns how accurate the agent is
Approving each purchase maximises the number of purchases agents make, since users like confirming each order
Requiring approval means the wallet no longer needs to hide card details from the agent or merchant
Approval for each purchase is the only way to support American Express, Mastercard and Visa together
questions.explanation: Agents making real payments is new and mistakes cost money. Starting with approval on every purchase limits damage while the team gathers data on accuracy and user trust. Later, spending limits can reduce friction once the agent proves reliable. This is a common way to stage autonomy.
rationales: Correct: it matches the stage of trust and lets the team learn before reducing friction.
Extra approvals add friction and usually lower purchase volume.
Hiding card details is a separate security measure, and the reports say it's still used.
Nothing in the reports says card networks require per-purchase approval.
questions.interview_tip: Current-events questions test whether you can explain a launch decision. Linking autonomy to trust and the cost of errors shows strong AI product thinking.
